definition: Penchant means a tendency, partiality, preference.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word penchant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know penchant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The station manager's penchant for rearranging furniture means no desk is ever where you left it on a Friday.
A liking is milder than a penchant — pleasant when it's satisfied, quiet when it isn't.
A craving goes further than a penchant — a penchant leans you toward the paprika; a craving marches you to the store at midnight.

A fondness is a warm liking you know you have — you would name it if asked. A penchant can steer you unnoticed: it is the standing tilt in your choices, visible to everyone but its owner. Fondness lives in the feelings; a penchant shows up in the pattern.

A weakness is a fondness you indulge a little guiltily — you know the pull is there and you give in anyway. A penchant needs neither guilt nor awareness: it simply tilts you the same way, time after time, whether or not you ever catch yourself doing it.

Penchant means a tendency, partiality, preference.
Chef Adeyemi has a penchant for smoked paprika — it turns up in the stew, the cornbread, and once, memorably, the lemonade.
A penchant is a standing pull toward something — stronger than a taste, more personal than a habit, and always aimed by 'for': a penchant for puns, for risky shortcuts, for paprika.
It needn't be chosen, and its owner is often the last to notice it.
Penchant dresses up 'liking' — use it when a leaning is habitual and worth remarking: a penchant for drama, for hats, for the last word.
It always takes 'for.' A fondness is warmer, a weakness more indulgent, a craving more urgent; a penchant simply tilts you, again and again, the same way.

The cartographer Elena Voss drew coastal charts for forty years, and until last winter nobody had noticed the thing they all have in common.
An archivist cataloguing her charts found it: wherever the coastline allowed it, Voss nudged her surveys to include one lighthouse more than the commission required.
Colleagues who knew her swear she never spoke of lighthouses.
Her field notebooks never brag about them; the extra tower simply appears, chart after chart, decade after decade.
It was, the archivist wrote, a penchant in its purest form — a tilt in the hand that its owner may never have seen.
The retrospective now hangs all forty charts in one room.
From the doorway, the pattern is unmistakable.
